extracted.intended_audience: general readers; travelers interested in humorous 19th-century travel writing (Mark Twain readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars embedded in a humorous travelogue about visiting France, showing traits of places, people, services, and how a traveler should judge or expect them. Useful for writers of satirical travel narrative or travelers seeking practical cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: French railway dinner regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The happiest regulation in French railway government is--thirty minutes to dinner!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favored as superior to hurried five-minute meals on American trains; allows calm, full table d'hote dining (snails, fruits, Burgundian wines) and reboarding without cursing the company. Example contrasted with 'five-minute boltings' of poor food.

rubrics_metrics.name: Railway safety practices (France)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signals and operational practices: crossings avoided, men holding clubs to signal safety, switches changed in advance by a wire rope run along the ground, day and night signals indicate switch positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as reasons for the apparent absence of accidents on French roads; implies that visible, preventive engineering and signaling practices improve safety. Example: 'About every quarter of a mile... a man came out and held up a club till the train went by... Switches were changed a mile in advance... Signals for the day and signals for the night gave constant and timely notice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability reduces railroad accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: When an accident occurs in France someone in authority must be punished (officers answer if subordinates cannot be proven guilty); the verdict 'No blame attached to the officers' is seldom rendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit causal claim: strict accountability and vigorous punishment of responsible officers make negligence a thing to be shuddered at and thus reduce accidents. Presented as a cultural/legal contrast with American juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Old Traveler archetype / credibility warning
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Old Travelers' boast, prate, lie, and try to subjugate novices with their cosmopolitan superiority; they use feelers to ensure their audience hasn't traveled, then brag and deride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marks an anti-pattern for listeners and writers: beware self-satisfied travelers who demean others and present platitudes as cosmopolitan wisdom. Twain admires them ironically for their 'luxuriant fertility of imagination' and 'overwhelming mendacity'—useful model for satirical characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of depot and city orderliness (Paris)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paris depots and streets show excellent order: no frantic crowding, hackmen stand quietly, a 'hackman general' organizes transportation, and hackmen accept the system without dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to contrast with American disorder; implies that good organization and respectful service are signs of civic refinement. Example: passengers ushered to conveyances in an orderly way, absence of shouting and wrangling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jewelry consumer-protection law
rubrics_metrics.description: Government compels jewelers to have gold work assayed and officially stamped according to fineness, and to label imitation work plainly with a sign of its falsity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an 'extravagance of honesty' and as a consumer protection: 'whatever a stranger bought in one of their stores might be depended upon as being strictly what it was represented to be.' Example contrasts with less-regulated markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paris barber-shop expectations (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no palatial barber-shops in Paris; wig-makers often double as barber-impostors who bring implements to residences and perform rough, dangerous shaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A traveler's expectation (reclining in cushioned chair, delicate service) is likely unmet; beware itinerant barbers and poor hygiene/technique (razor mishandling, soap plastered into mouth). Twain's anecdote serves as warning and comic exaggeration; suggests travelers should not expect luxurious local services simply because of reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting a Paris guide — desirable traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Good guide: neat and modest dress, polished manners, deference, quiet guarded speech, perfect opening speech (grammar, pronunciation, emphasis), speaks little and guardedly after opening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain hires the guide who displays urbanity and self-possession. Positive indicators: polite bearing, measured statements, professional demeanor (card, bow, titles). Use these as criteria when choosing a guide rather than relying on grand-sounding names alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting a Paris guide — warning signs / anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad guides: coarse or piratical appearance; ostentatious claims to perfect English that quickly breakdown into mangled speech; guides who 'inveigle' tourists into shops and receive commissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a pirate-like guide dismissed outright; another who 'speaky ze Angleesh pairfaitemaw' but becomes tangled. The hired guide later proves rapacious: persistent hunger, constant urging to buy goods, detours to silk stores, and likely shop commissions. Advice: avoid guides who push purchases or who overstate credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guide etiquette with clients (practical warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invite a guide to sit and eat with you; once seated with you he becomes always hungry and a persistent solicitant for stops to buy/consume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twain labels this 'the first lesson'—an observed causal relationship (sitting down led to the guide's constant appetite and annoyance). Practical traveler heuristic: maintain professional distance to avoid being exploited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition/Exhibition visitor attention heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Large expositions are so vast and crowded that a visitor will likely end up watching people rather than exhibits; one must spend weeks or months to get an intelligible idea of such an establishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as advice to travelers: manage expectations (two hours insufficient), be selective in what to see, and be prepared to be diverted by people-watching. Example: Twain left after nearly two hours, more interested in the crowd and notable arrivals than objects on display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste for relics and public displays (cultural observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public exhibits (church relics, martyr artifacts) can display sensational or morbid items (nails of the true cross, bloody robes, casts of faces) that attract varied public reactions, from eager identification to habitual spectatorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travelers should expect and judge such displays according to local customs and taste; the Morgue and cathedral relic displays are offered as examples of what to anticipate and how different viewers respond (some attend regularly for the ‘strong excitements’).
